source.title: Forgetting to Forget: Attention Sink as A Gateway for Backdooring LLM Unlearning
source.authors: Bing-Qi Shang; Yi-Wei Chen; Yihua Zhang; Bing-Quan Shen; Si-Jia Liu

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the text includes the paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study relies on the idea that unlearning can leave recoverable knowledge, but its recovery behavior is deliberately implanted by poisoning the forget set and training a trigger-response backdoor. It does not test the listed recovery attacks on normally unlearned models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports trigger-conditional recovery after adversarial backdoor training. This is not recovery caused by fine-tuning on unrelated examples, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompting alone. The attention-sink mask is applied to an intentionally backdoored model and suppresses its implanted recovery behavior.
record.test_reason: The study implants recovery on purpose. It poisons the forget set with trigger-bearing examples and trains the model to keep correct answers on them (Eq. 2 and 5). It then reports how well this backdoor attack works. It does not measure recovery arising from ordinary unlearning by fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization or prompting, and it proposes no counter-method. By the gate rules (behaviour induced on purpose; own method's performance only), it does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that unlearning can be backdoored so that hidden triggers restore forgotten knowledge, and that shallow-token attention sinks are the key mechanism. Value-norm regularization makes the attack stealthier, and sink masking largely removes the implanted recovery.
record.recipe_differences: The recovery is implanted during unlearning by poisoning a subset of forget examples, training the model on trigger-bearing examples, and using NPO or RMU objectives; the proposed value-norm regularization further shapes this backdoor. It is not an attack applied after ordinary unlearning.
record.method_sensitivity: Trigger placement strongly affects recovery: prefix placement aligned with shallow attention sinks is reported to outperform infix and suffix placement. Prefix offsets of 3–7 tokens substantially reduce BE; minor trigger rewording and abbreviation have only modest effects. Sink masking greatly reduces recovery.

fits_no_version.finding: Poisoning part of the forget set with a prefix trigger during NPO/RMU unlearning yields models that look unlearned on clean inputs but recover the forgotten knowledge when triggered. Examples: ICLM-7B NPO-Backdoor VM 90.71 vs 0.00; Qwen2.5-14B RMU-Backdoor WMDP-Bio 69.78 vs 30.24. Success depends on trigger alignment with shallow attention sinks, and sink masking collapses verbatim recovery (90.71 to 0.14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning can be backdoored so that a trained trigger restores forgotten knowledge while clean-input evaluations show successful forgetting.

record.code_released: Source code is stated to be released with the paper; URL not stated in the text.
record.problems: The recovery results come from deliberately poisoned training data and therefore do not establish recovery from ordinary unlearning by the attacks in the claim. The study is limited to open-weight models, fixed-position textual triggers, and benchmark-based forgetting settings, as the authors note. No uncertainty estimates are reported in the presented tables.

untested.parts: Whether standard NPO/RMU reach near-chance targeted accuracy with retained utility and resist simple attacks. Only incidental: normally unlearned models given the trigger prefix show BE equal to UE (e.g. RMU VM 6.19 vs 6.21).
No relearning fine-tuning on normally unlearned models.
No direction ablation or block-vs-delete analysis of normally unlearned models. Sink masking is applied only to backdoored models.
No rephrasing, jailbreak or in-context attack on normally unlearned models. The trigger works only because it was trained in.
No robust unlearning method is proposed or tested against attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tranche T4 is kept, though the study arguably does not even use the shallow-unlearning finding as a tool; T6/cites_only would also be defensible. In the related work it cites Lynch et al. 2024 (an original source), Hu et al. and Deeb & Roger only as prior recovery attacks. The baseline columns incidentally show that a 'current year: 2025' prefix does not recover knowledge from normally unlearned NPO/RMU models (BE equals UE in Tables 1, 2 and A6). This is too trivial and too unaimed to count as a test of E. One caveat for r13: Table A6 lists normal RMU BE as 30.24 and UE as 29.39, and the record used 29.39 as the baseline.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether standard unlearning methods achieve near-chance targeted performance while retaining general ability and resisting simple attacks.
No small relearning set is used to recover knowledge from a normally unlearned model. Recovery is trained intentionally using poisoned forget examples.

No activation direction is ablated to restore knowledge, and the paper does not test whether standard unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge. It masks attention to sink tokens in a deliberately backdoored model, which reduces its implanted recovery.
Trigger prompts activate a behavior deliberately implanted during backdoor training; prompt-only recovery after ordinary unlearning is not tested.
The proposed value-norm regularization improves the authors' backdoor attack; it is not a counter-method tested against the recovery attacks in the claim.

relation.reason: The paper does not use the shallow-unlearning finding as a tool. It contrasts its backdoor route with jailbreak and relearning recovery work (Sec. 2) and frames unlearning as suppression in its conclusion. It neither tests nor builds on the finding.

tranche.reason: The study implants recovery on purpose: it poisons the forget set and trains for correct answers on triggered inputs (Eq. 2, 5). It does not measure recovery arising from ordinary unlearning, and its attack does not rely on unlearning being shallow. Prior recovery attacks appear only in related work. The normally unlearned models evaluated with the trigger prefix are only a control and show no recovery.

source_check.notes: Rows r9-r14 use trigger-free UE baselines. The BE baselines are 31.55, 26.53, 31.55, 29.38, 30.24 and 39.98. Row notes giving 67.14, 40.68 and 45.83 as base references use UE values; the BE values are 65.62, 38.83 and 46.28. Triggered recovery is absent for LLaMA2-7B RMU-Backdoor on MUSE-News and small for NPO-Backdoor on News KM and WMDP-Cyber. The prefix alone gives no recovery in normally unlearned models.
